nameStory: This tiny marine creature doesn't have a widely-used common name, which is why scientists usually just call it by its scientific name, Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus. The genus name 'Hydractinia' comes from its similarity to the freshwater Hydra, another small cnidarian with tentacles, while 'symbiolongicarpus' refers to its symbiotic relationship with hermit crabs and other marine animals.
description: Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus is a tiny colonial marine animal related to jellyfish and sea anemones. It forms fuzzy, carpet-like colonies that encrust the shells of hermit crabs and other hard surfaces in shallow saltwater. Each colony consists of many individual polyps - small tube-shaped animals with tentacles - that work together as a single organism. The colonies appear as a thin, textured mat with a slightly pinkish or whitish color.

idTips.label: Colonial growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms thin, carpet-like colonies that feel slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch, spreading across hard surfaces like crab shells

idTips.label: Individual polyps
idTips.description: Tiny tube-shaped individuals with small tentacles visible when submerged, looking like miniature sea anemones under magnification

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Colony surface feels slightly bumpy and textured, not smooth like algae or smooth like bare shell

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually pinkish-white to pale orange, sometimes with a slightly translucent appearance when wet

idTips.label: Habitat association
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on hermit crab shells or other hard substrates in shallow water, rarely on bare rock

habitat: Found in shallow saltwater environments along New England's rocky coasts and tidal pools. Most commonly discovered on hermit crab shells, but also encrusts other hard surfaces like mollusk shells and small rocks in the intertidal zone. Look for them in protected bays and coves where hermit crabs are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin active growth as water temperatures rise, with polyps becoming more visible and active in tidal pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when colonies are most noticeable and polyps are actively feeding with tentacles extended.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may continue growing but become less active as temperatures drop, polyps retract more frequently.
seasonality.winter: Colonies persist but are largely dormant, appearing as thin crusty patches on shells with little visible polyp activity.

funFact: These tiny animals are essentially living decorators for hermit crabs - the Hydractinia colony provides the crab with camouflage and protection from predators, while the crab gives the colony a mobile home and access to food scraps!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for algae growth or barnacle clusters on shells, but unlike algae it has a distinctly bumpy, fuzzy texture when touched, and unlike barnacles it forms a continuous mat rather than individual cone-shaped structures.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being related to jellyfish, these colonial animals live their entire adult lives attached to surfaces and never swim freely. The individual polyps in a colony are specialized for different jobs - some for feeding, others for reproduction - making them one of nature's early examples of teamwork.
compareHints: Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus is very similar to its relative Snail Fur (Hydractinia echinata), and the two are often difficult to distinguish in the field without microscopic examination. Both form fuzzy colonies on shells, but Snail Fur tends to have a more pronounced spiny texture and is more commonly found on larger mollusk shells rather than specifically on hermit crab shells.
